title: sfrecord~ does not start at a fixed distance from the message that starts it: 1 to 9 signal vectors, 1.3 to 12.0 ms
set: empty set, four tracks, no clips; the device on audio track index 2
question: How far does sfrecord~ lag the message that starts it, and is that lag a constant that grid bound transcription could calibrate out?

answers.answered_in: A question raised in working notes kept outside the repository, under "3. Die Max-for-Live-"Hoeren"-Idee". This record is the published answer.

method: A count~ inside the device counts samples from the moment live.thisdevice reports the device alive. It is never restarted, so it is a clock both ends of a measurement can read.
That counter drives a one sample impulse every 48000 samples into sfrecord~'s only inlet. The impulses therefore sit at known multiples of the period on that clock.
On the start message the device reads the counter through snapshot~ and reports it, then starts the recorder. On the stop message it stops the recorder and reports the counter again.

The recording is read back in Python. The first impulse in the file sits at file index k, and the impulse it came from sits at a multiple of the period, so sample zero of the file is fixed to (multiple - k) and the latency is that minus the reported counter. The period is longer than any plausible latency, so the modulo has one solution.
Twelve runs of two seconds each, back to back, in one session with nothing else running in the set.
guards: A run is discarded unless the counter advanced between the two marks, the recording holds at least one impulse, and every impulse spacing equals the period. The first attempt failed all three at once and reported a latency of zero: count~ constructs switched off, so the counter stood at 0, every sample was 0 modulo the period, and the impulse train was a constant 1.0. Without the guards that run reads as a clean zero latency measurement.
All twelve runs of the reported sample passed all three.

readings.counter_and_recorder_agree: On a three second run the counter advanced 299456 -> 443840, a difference of 144384, and the file held exactly 144384 frames. The clock the latency is measured against is the same clock the recorder writes on.

earlier_sample.note: Five readings taken before the repeat option existed, at two and three seconds, agree: 575, 575, 447, 191, 575. They are not part of the twelve above.

result: sfrecord~ starts late, and by a varying amount. Across twelve runs the start landed between 63 and 575 samples after the counter reading, which is 1.3 to 12.0 ms at 48 kHz.
Every single reading is one less than a multiple of 64. The latency is therefore quantised to Live's 64 sample signal vector and the spread is a whole number of vectors, from one to nine.
The lag is not a constant. A fixed offset cannot calibrate it out, because the offset would be wrong by up to eight vectors on the next recording.

For grid bound transcription this means the recording has to carry its own time reference. Either a marker recorded into the signal, or the counter read at the first sample rather than at the message.

consequences.sound_rebuild_spec: Group A's audio_transcribe_drums cannot be calibrated by measuring this latency once and subtracting it.
consequences.instrument_sweep_spec: The same applies to any probe that plays a note at a known time and records the result.

scope_and_weakness: One machine, one Live version, one audio device, one buffer size, one session. Live's audio preferences were not varied, and the signal vector is exactly the quantity this measures against.
Twelve runs is enough to prove the lag is not constant and not enough to describe its distribution. Nothing here says whether 575 is a ceiling.
The set was empty and no other plug-in was running. A loaded set is the case that matters for transcription and was not measured.

snapshot~ reads the counter at the last signal vector boundary and the recorder starts at the next one, so one vector at each end is the floor under any single reading. The spread reported here is nine vectors wide and survives that floor; a claim about any individual value would not.
The direction is assumed, not proved: a latency is read modulo the period, so a recording that began before the message would read as a very large positive number. None did.
recorded_also_in_note: This record is the only published account of the measurement. What it also went into at the time were working notes kept outside the repository.
